subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Poem — Read-Aloud and First Response

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the textbook to the poem on pp. 1–2 and invites students to look at any illustration while she reads the title aloud. Students predict what the poem might be about.
Teacher reads the full poem aloud expressively, pausing after each couplet. Students listen with books open and follow along silently.
Teacher reads the poem a second time, this time inviting students to join in on the rhyming words at the end of each line — an unhurried shared experience.
Class discusses in brief: what did they notice about the rhyming words? Teacher writes the rhyme pairs (tall/fall, sing/anything) on the board and reads them together one more time chorally.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's end-rhyme scheme (tall/fall, sing/anything, share/there, near/cheer, one/begun) creates a chant-like quality — lean into this in the read-aloud by slowing down at each line-end. Students new to the poem benefit from hearing it at least twice before any discussion; resist rushing to comprehension questions.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.2): answer questions on joining hands and helping each other.

time_bands.activity: Students open to the poem (pp. 1–2). Teacher leads a brisk choral reading of all five couplets, pointing to each line. The class repeats as a group, keeping the rhythm steady.
Let us Think — A. (p.2): teacher poses the first question — what happens when you join hands with your team — and takes several student responses, anchoring answers to lines in the poem.
Teacher poses the second question — why is helping each other important — and guides students to connect the poem's imagery of joined hands and shared victories to their own experience.
Class recites the closing couplet together: “Together we shine, our hearts as one, / For in our team, the joy’s begun!” Teacher invites one student to say in a single sentence what the poem is about.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the poem together, students can now connect its images — joined hands, shared cheer — to their answers. A common difficulty at this stage is treating comprehension as a memory exercise; prompt students to point to the line that helped them answer.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss — Experiences of Joy and Teamwork

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak — B. (p.2): guided discussion on joy, shared activities, and losing a game.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the discussion frame: the poem says “win or lose, we always share” — what does sharing a loss feel like? Students turn to a partner briefly.

Let us Think + Let us Speak — B. (p.2): teacher takes responses to the first two discussion prompts — what makes you feel joyful, and what good activity can you do with a friend. Several pairs share with the class.

Let us Think + Let us Speak — B. (p.2): teacher poses the third prompt — have you ever lost a game and how did you feel. Students respond in full sentences; teacher models a sentence frame if needed: “When I lost, I felt…”

Brief class share-out: teacher invites two or three students to tell the class one thing they discovered about their partner. Teacher closes by connecting responses to the poem’s message of shared experience.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s joyful, affirming tone sets a safe atmosphere for discussing loss; remind students that the poem itself says losing is part of teamwork. Keep responses to the first two prompts brisk so there is enough time for the richer third prompt about losing.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.2): role-play the Bokali–Darsana dialogue and share favourite food and festival.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Bokali–Darsana exchange aloud once, then reads it again with a student volunteer taking one role. Class listens and observes the sentence structure.
Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.2): pairs practise the scripted exchange — each student plays one speaker, then they swap roles. Teacher circulates and listens, offering brief pronunciation support.

Students extend the conversation using the sentence frame (Hello, I am ___. My favourite food is ___. My favourite festival is ___. In this festival, ___.). Each partner shares their lines; teacher invites two or three pairs to perform for the class.
Class reflects briefly: what did they learn about their partner’s food or festival that surprised them? Teacher links this to the poem’s idea that different people stand together in unity.

periods.teacher_notes: The dialogue names Bokali and Darsana as speakers who celebrate diversity in food, festivals, and languages — this personal sharing deepens the poem’s unity theme. Students who are shy about performing may benefit from keeping their books open during the role-play.

periods.activity_title: Team Leader Discussion — Uniting a Disagreeing Team

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak — B. (p.2): fourth prompt — what would you do as team leader when teammates disagree.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the scene from the poem: the poem talks about team spirit filling the air with cheer — but what happens before cheer, when two teammates disagree? Students listen and consider.

Let us Think + Let us Speak — B. (p.2): teacher poses the fourth prompt — imagine you are team leader and two teammates disagree; what would you do to unite the team again. Small groups of three discuss for a few minutes, then each group nominates a spokesperson.
Spokespersons share their group’s ideas with the class. Teacher writes key strategies on the board — listen, talk it out, find a common goal — and links each to a line or image from the poem.
Teacher invites students to say the line “With each hand joined, the goal is near” aloud together as a closing thought about resolving disagreements through unity.

periods.teacher_notes: This prompt asks for reasoning and strategy, making it the most cognitively demanding of the four discussion questions — giving groups time to talk before the share-out is essential. Anchor the debrief firmly to the poem’s imagery (joined hands, shared goal) so the discussion stays connected to the text.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (pp. 3–4): fill collective nouns for sheep, wolves, flowers, trees, bees, boys, and keys using the word box.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces collective nouns by connecting them to the poem: “The poem is about a team — what are some words for a group of things?” Teacher elicits a few examples and writes ‘a flock of birds’ on the board.

Students open to pp. 3–4. Teacher walks through each illustration slowly — sheep, wolves, flowers, trees, bees, boys, keys — asking students to look at the picture and predict the word before checking the box.
Let us Learn — A. (pp. 3–4): students complete the fill-in individually. Teacher circulates, prompting students to say each completed phrase aloud: “a herd of sheep”.
Class checks answers together. Teacher says each collective noun and asks the class to name two or three other things that group could describe — building word range beyond the exercise.

periods.teacher_notes: Collective nouns echo the poem’s central motif of togetherness — a swarm, a choir, a pack are all images of unity. Students often confuse herd, pack, and swarm; reinforcing each with a clear animal picture and an oral sentence (“a swarm of bees”) reduces this error.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (p.5): fill prepositions of place — behind, between, near, in front of — using the town map.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple two-building sketch on the board and demonstrates ‘behind’, ‘in front of’, ‘near’, and ‘between’ with gestures and labels. Students repeat each preposition after the teacher.

Students open to the town map on p.5. Teacher walks the class through the map, naming each building (hospital, school, bank, post office, bookstore, Children’s Park) and asking “what is next to the hospital?” before the exercise begins.

Let us Learn — B. (p.5): students complete the four blanks individually, choosing from the word box. Teacher circulates and asks individual students to read their completed sentence aloud to confirm understanding.
Class checks answers together, with the teacher pointing to the map for each sentence. Students who disagree with an answer are invited to explain their reasoning using the map.

periods.teacher_notes: Prepositions of place are taught here through the map’s visual grammar — where buildings stand relative to one another — rather than as an isolated rule. A common error is confusing ‘behind’ and ‘in front of’ when the map’s orientation differs from the child’s own viewpoint; ask students to point with a finger before writing.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (pp. 6–7): describe what Lubang and Obang–Manya–Tina are doing and what will happen next.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens pp. 6–7 and walks the class through all five helping scenes slowly — Lubang and his injured friend, the classroom clean-up group, Anna and the old lady, the art project with the child in a wheelchair, and the classroom with raised hands. Students observe and name what they see.

Teacher models writing for the first scene on the board: “Lubang is supporting his injured friend so that he can walk. Next, they will go to the nurse’s room together.” Teacher points out the two-part structure: what is happening now, what will happen next.

Let us Write — A. (pp. 6–7): students write their own responses to scenes 2 and 3 (Obang, Manya and Tina; Anna and the old lady) in their notebooks, using the same two-part structure. Teacher circulates and gives brief oral feedback on sentence clarity.
Two or three students share their sentences for scene 2 or 3 aloud. Teacher highlights strong two-part responses and invites any quick corrections as a group.

periods.teacher_notes: The five pictures all show acts of helping, mirroring the poem’s theme of supporting one another — this is a good moment to remind students of the poem’s line “helping each other, we never fall”. Keep the writing frame simple (what is happening now + what will happen next) so students focus on content rather than structure.

periods.activity_title: Picture-Prompted Writing — Completing the Helping Scenes

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (pp. 6–7): describe the wheelchair art project and the classroom raise-hands scenes; revise and share.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the two-part sentence frame from the picture-writing work (what is happening, what will happen next). Two volunteers read a sentence they wrote for scene 2 or 3 aloud — this warms the class up for today’s writing.

Teacher models writing for scene 4 (Zakir, Gulpreet and Gilashree doing the art project with the child in a wheelchair) on the board, thinking aloud about choosing a precise verb: “paint together” not just “do art”.

Let us Write — A. (pp. 6–7): students write responses to scenes 4 and 5 (the art project; students raising hands in class) individually. Teacher circulates and asks students to read their sentences aloud quietly to themselves before finalising.

Pairs swap notebooks and read each other’s sentences for one scene. Each reader tells their partner one thing they liked and one word they found interesting. Teacher closes by noting that every scene shows a different kind of teamwork.

periods.teacher_notes: Having practised the two-part frame on scenes 1–3, students are ready to apply it more independently here. The scene with the child in a wheelchair is an opportunity to affirm inclusive teamwork — the poem’s ‘bond of trust’ applies here as much as anywhere.

periods.activity_title: Do You Know — Honeybees and Ants as Team Workers

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Do You Know + Let us Do (p.3–4 area): discuss honeybee waggle dance and ant teamwork as examples of togetherness in nature.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Do You Know passage aloud: honeybees use a waggle dance to share the location of flowers; ants work as a team using signals to find food and build nests. Students listen and visualise.

Do You Know + Let us Do: teacher asks: “How is a bee’s waggle dance like the poem’s idea of team spirit filling the air?” Students discuss in pairs, then share. Teacher writes the key comparison on the board.

Students discuss: if ants use signals and bees use a dance, what ‘signals’ do people use to work as a team? Students name examples — a nod, a cheer, raising a hand — connecting human teamwork to animal teamwork.

Teacher closes with a brief oral riddle: “I waggle to tell my friends where to fly — what am I?” Students respond. Teacher links back to the poem’s image of voices cheering together as a human equivalent of the bee’s dance.

periods.teacher_notes: The Do You Know passage extends the poem’s teamwork theme into the natural world — honeybees and ants are concrete, accessible exemplars of collective effort. Students are often fascinated by the waggle dance; resist spending too long here and use their curiosity to drive the comparison discussion rather than explaining the biology in detail.
materials: Textbook pp. 3–4 area (Do You Know passage)

periods.activity_title: Let Us Do — Create a Symbol of Togetherness

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Do You Know + Let us Do (pp. 3–4 area): fold, draw, cut and colour a paper togetherness figure; share the finished symbol.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Let Us Do instructions aloud: fold paper, draw one side of a body, cut along the outline, unfold, and colour. Teacher demonstrates the fold and the outline drawing on a sheet of plain paper at the front.

Do You Know + Let us Do (pp. 3–4 area): students follow the five steps — fold, draw, cut, unfold, colour — at their own pace. Teacher circulates to help with the fold or the cutting. Students choose their own colours.

Students hold up or pass their finished figures. Teacher invites each student to say in one sentence what their symbol looks like and what it represents for them: “My symbol shows two people holding hands and it means…”
Teacher closes by displaying a few figures together on the board ledge and reading the poem’s last line — “For in our team, the joy’s begun!” — as a collective closing moment.

periods.teacher_notes: Students should complete their figure — drawing, cutting, colouring, and sharing — entirely within this unit; no materials or unfinished work need carry over. The craft step of unfolding the paper to reveal a chain of figures is the moment of discovery — give students time to notice it before moving to sharing.
materials: Textbook pp. 3–4 area (Let Us Do instructions)

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis — Togetherness Across Words, Voices and Actions

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites the class to recite the poem ‘Together We Can’ from memory or from the book, chorally. After the recitation, teacher asks: “Which line do you like most and why?” — two or three students respond briefly.

Quick word-game: teacher calls out a category — animals, people, plants — and students race to name the correct collective noun. Examples drawn from the chapter: a swarm, a herd, a pack, a bouquet, a grove, a choir. Students keep score as a team.

Pairs retell the chapter’s journey in four sentences: the poem’s message, one collective noun they remember, one helping scene from the pictures, and one thing they made or talked about. Each pair shares with the pair beside them.

Independent writing: students write two sentences connecting the chapter to their own life — one about a time they worked as part of a team and one about how it felt. Teacher writes the frame: “Once, my team and I ___. It felt ___.”

Teacher closes with a riddle: “I waggle to guide my team, I rhyme when I cheer, I show togetherness when you unfold me — what am I?” (answers: a bee’s dance, the poem, the paper figure). Students call out answers and celebrate the chapter together.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the poem’s themes, the collective-noun and preposition work, the helping scenes, and the nature extension — students who have encountered any part of the chapter will have something to contribute. The closing riddle bundles the three strands of the chapter (poem, word work, craft) into one playful moment of recognition.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 1 beginning “Together we stand, strong and tall”. Which word in the first two lines rhymes with 'tall'?

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this may be selecting any rhyming-sounding word from the poem without checking the first couplet.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student scanned for a word that sounds pleasant rather than one that matches the specific couplet.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals the student may have looked at a later stanza rather than the opening lines.

items.item_stem: The last two lines of the poem say that joy begins in a team. In one or two sentences, explain what you think the poem is telling us about why working together matters.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The poem tells us that when people work together and support one another, they become stronger and happier than they would be alone; the joy and cheer that come from teamwork are shared by everyone.

items.item_stem: In the Bokali and Darsana conversation, Bokali says that people in his country have different traditions, food, festivals, and languages but still stand in unity. Which of the following best describes what Bokali means?

options.label: A
options.text: People who share the same food always get along.

options.label: B
options.text: Differences in traditions and language do not stop people from being united.

options.label: C
options.text: Darsana and Bokali live in the same place.

options.label: D
options.text: Unity is only possible when everyone speaks the same language.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a literal reading focused on food rather than the broader idea of diversity and unity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student focused on the names rather than the content of what Bokali says.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows the student has inverted Bokali’s message — he is saying unity exists despite language differences.

expected_elements: Listens to both friends without taking sides.

Uses calm, positive language to encourage teamwork.
